title: The Pope in Argentina, hacked fridges and a 100-year pitch drop

stories.headline: Pope Leo draws record Buenos Aires crowd and warns against austerity
stories.headlineZh: 教皇良十四世在布宜诺斯艾利斯吸引创纪录人潮，并警示紧缩政策
stories.summaryZh: 约250万人参加教皇露天弥撒，他敦促米莱政府不要以严厉紧缩惩罚穷人。
stories.c1:
Pope Leo XIV has drawn what appears to be the largest crowd of his papacy, with Buenos Aires officials estimating that around 2.5 million people attended an open-air Mass at the Monumento de los Españoles on Monday. Some pilgrims had travelled more than 1,000 kilometres to be there, and many camped overnight along the capital's broad avenues in the hope of catching a glimpse of him.

The visit forms the second leg of a 12-day tour of Latin America and is the first by a pope to Argentina since 1987. Leo, who was born in Chicago, spent decades as a missionary in South America, so the region is familiar territory. In his sermon, he welcomed the turnout in a part of the world that has long been a Catholic stronghold but is losing ground to fast-growing evangelical churches.

Yet the trip has not been purely spiritual. A day before the Mass, the Pope urged Argentinians to protect their democracy and called on President Javier Milei's government not to punish the poor with harsh austerity. Milei, a libertarian, has come under fire for cutting subsidies, laying off public servants and scaling back welfare, including disability benefits. Leo also endorsed measures that create opportunities and encourage private initiative, provided that the benefits of growth reach the disadvantaged, a line that drew applause.

The issue surfaced again when he visited the Pequeño Cottolengo, a home for abandoned people with disabilities in the suburb of Claypole. He told residents and staff that people with disabilities are "a blessing, not a burden" on society, and suggested that a nation's progress can be measured by how it welcomes those with particular needs. Given the concerns raised by disability groups and Church leaders about cuts to assistance programs, his words touched a sensitive nerve.
stories.b2:
Pope Leo XIV has attracted the biggest crowd of his time as pope so far. Buenos Aires officials say about 2.5 million people came to an outdoor Mass in the city on Monday. Some people travelled more than 1,000 kilometres, and many slept outside overnight to get a good view.

Argentina is the second stop on the Pope's 12-day tour of Latin America. It is the first visit by a pope to the country since 1987. Leo was born in Chicago, but he worked as a missionary in South America for many years. In his sermon, he said he was happy to see so many Catholics in a region where evangelical churches are growing quickly.

The visit also had a political side. A day before the Mass, the Pope asked Argentinians to protect their democracy. He also asked President Javier Milei's government not to hurt poor people with strict spending cuts. Milei has been criticised for cutting subsidies, public sector jobs and welfare, including disability payments.

Later, the Pope visited a home for people with disabilities in the suburb of Claypole. He said people with disabilities are a blessing for society, not a burden. Disability groups and Church leaders have been worried about cuts to support programs, so his words were important to many people.

vocab.en: a situation or subject you already know well

vocab.en: a place where a belief or group has strong support
vocab.example: The inner suburbs have long been a stronghold for the Greens.

vocab.en: to become less popular, successful or powerful
vocab.example: Print newspapers continue to lose ground to online news.

vocab.en: to be strongly criticised
vocab.example: The council came under fire for closing the local library.

vocab.en: to reduce the size or amount of something
vocab.example: The company decided to scale back its expansion plans.

vocab.en: strict cuts to government spending
vocab.example: Years of austerity left many public hospitals short of staff.

vocab.en: only if a particular condition is met
vocab.example: You can borrow my car, provided that you fill up the tank.

vocab.en: to mention something that upsets people because it matters to them
vocab.example: Her comment about rent prices clearly touched a nerve with the audience.

questions.q: Around 2.5 million people attended the Pope's Mass in Buenos Aires, according to city officials.
questions.explain: 原文称 Buenos Aires officials estimating that around 2.5 million people attended，与题干一致，故为True。

questions.q: This is the first time Pope Leo XIV has ever been to South America.
questions.explain: 原文称他 spent decades as a missionary in South America，说明他早已在南美生活多年，与题干矛盾，故为False。

questions.q: President Milei personally attended the open-air Mass on Monday.
questions.explain: 原文只提到教皇对米莱政府的呼吁，并未说明米莱是否出席弥撒，故为Not Given。

questions.q: Why did the Pope's words at the Pequeño Cottolengo touch a sensitive nerve?
options: Because the home had recently been closed by the government
Because there were concerns about cuts to assistance programs
Because he refused to meet Church leaders
questions.explain: 原文称 Given the concerns raised by disability groups and Church leaders about cuts to assistance programs，故选B。

stories.discuss: Should religious leaders comment on a government's economic policies, or should they stay out of politics? Why do you think so?

stories.headline: France blames Iran for hacking supermarket fridges and sparking fires
stories.headlineZh: 法国指控伊朗黑客入侵超市冷柜并引发火灾
stories.summaryZh: 法国称伊朗革命卫队网络部队远程调高冷柜温度，致食品变质、起火，将寻求欧洲制裁。
stories.c1:
France has formally accused a cyber unit linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of sabotaging refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets, in what officials describe as an unprecedented attack on everyday infrastructure. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned and that France would push for sanctions at a European level.

According to investigators, the hackers gained access to internet-connected cooling systems overnight on 11 and 12 October and remotely raised temperatures to as high as 50°C. Retailers estimate that millions of euros' worth of food was spoiled, and in some stores the heat was intense enough to spark fires or melt equipment. Several major chains were caught up in the attack, among them Intermarché and Netto, which together had at least 300 stores affected, Coopérative U and Carrefour.

The Paris prosecutor's office has requested international arrest warrants for the leader of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit tied to the Revolutionary Guards, and two of his deputies. Investigators reportedly traced the intrusion through the use of Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices in Iran. Barrot called it the first large-scale cyberattack for sabotage purposes on French soil.

The incident has raised uncomfortable questions about how vulnerable ordinary connected devices may be. On 2 November, supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden also reported sudden overnight temperature spikes, affecting dozens of stores and a food distribution hub, although responsibility for those cases has yet to be established. Arguably, the episode shows that in an age of smart equipment, even a freezer aisle can become a target in a geopolitical conflict.
stories.b2:
France says a cyber unit connected to Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked the refrigeration systems of hundreds of supermarkets. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said France had called in the Iranian ambassador and would ask for sanctions across Europe.

Investigators say the hackers got into internet-connected cooling systems on the nights of 11 and 12 October. They raised the temperatures to as high as 50°C. Shops say food worth millions of euros was ruined. In some stores, the heat caused fires or melted equipment. Big chains such as Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U and Carrefour were affected.

The Paris prosecutor's office wants international arrest warrants for the leader of a cyber unit called Shahid Kaveh and two of his deputies. Investigators say the attackers used Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices in Iran. Barrot said it was the first large cyberattack aimed at sabotage in France.

The attack has made people worry about the safety of everyday connected machines. On 2 November, supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden also had sudden temperature rises overnight. Dozens of stores and a food distribution centre were affected, but it is not yet clear who was behind those problems.

vocab.example: The city faced unprecedented demand for public housing last winter.

vocab.en: to try hard to make something happen
vocab.example: Residents are pushing for a new bus route to the hospital.

vocab.en: to manage to enter a place or system

vocab.en: to cause something to start suddenly

vocab.en: involved in a situation without wanting to be

vocab.en: to find the origin of something by careful investigation

vocab.en: to make people think about difficult or worrying issues
vocab.example: The report raises uncomfortable questions about how the money was spent.

vocab.en: not proven or confirmed so far
vocab.example: The cause of the outage is yet to be established.

vocab.en: used when giving an opinion you think can be supported
vocab.example: She is arguably the best coach the club has ever had.

questions.q: The hackers raised the temperature inside the cooling systems to as high as 50°C.
questions.explain: 原文称 remotely raised temperatures to as high as 50°C，与题干一致，故为True。

questions.q: Investigators have confirmed that the same Iranian unit was behind the problems in Belgium and Sweden.
questions.explain: 原文称 responsibility for those cases has yet to be established，即尚未确定，与题干“已确认”矛盾，故为False。

questions.q: Iran has denied any involvement in the supermarket attacks.
questions.explain: 原文没有提到伊朗是否否认参与，故为Not Given。

questions.q: What action has the Paris prosecutor's office taken?
options: It has closed the affected supermarkets
It has fined the Iranian ambassador
It has requested international arrest warrants
questions.explain: 原文称 The Paris prosecutor's office has requested international arrest warrants，故选C。

stories.discuss: As more household and business devices connect to the internet, are the benefits worth the security risks? How should governments and companies respond?

stories.headline: World's longest-running science experiment nears its 100th birthday
stories.headlineZh: 世界上持续时间最长的科学实验即将迎来一百周年
stories.summaryZh: 昆士兰大学沥青滴落实验将满百年，九滴沥青落下却无人亲眼见证，第十滴或在几年内落下。
stories.c1:
Tucked behind glass outside a lecture theatre at the University of Queensland, a lump of black pitch is approaching a remarkable milestone. Officially the world's longest-running science experiment, the pitch drop experiment will turn 100 in 2027, and in all that time not a single falling drop has been seen by human eyes.

The experiment was set up by Thomas Parnell, the university's first professor of physics, to demonstrate the unusual properties of pitch, a substance then widely used to waterproof boats and household containers. In 1927 he heated a batch, sealed it in a glass funnel and left it to cool. Three years later he cut off the bottom of the funnel, and the pitch began to flow at an almost imperceptible pace.

According to its current custodian, Professor Andrew White, pitch looks like a solid but behaves like a liquid, rather like toothpaste, only billions of times more viscous. He estimates it moves at roughly an atom per second, more than 10 times slower than continental drift. Nine drops have fallen since 1930, yet each has managed to slip past its observers. In 1979, his predecessor John Mainstone stayed on campus over a weekend, only for a drop to fall after he had gone home; a power cut later foiled an attempt to capture one on camera.

The most recent drop, in 2014, never fell cleanly because the beaker beneath was already crowded with earlier pitch, so it spent about eight years slowly sagging. A fresh beaker is now in place, and White expects the tenth drop within the next couple of years. He would love to witness it, he admits, but would settle for a really good recording.
stories.b2:
At the University of Queensland, a piece of black pitch sits behind glass outside a lecture theatre. It is officially the world's longest-running science experiment, and it will turn 100 in 2027. In all that time, nobody has ever seen a drop fall.

Thomas Parnell, the university's first professor of physics, started the experiment to show how strange pitch is. In 1927 he heated some pitch, put it in a glass funnel and let it cool. Three years later he cut off the bottom of the funnel, and the pitch slowly started to flow.

Professor Andrew White now looks after the experiment. He says pitch looks solid but acts like a liquid, a bit like toothpaste, but billions of times thicker. It moves about an atom per second. Nine drops have fallen since 1930, but nobody has seen one. In 1979, John Mainstone waited at the university all weekend, but the drop fell after he went home.

The last drop, in 2014, did not fall properly because the beaker underneath was full of old pitch. Now there is a new, empty beaker, and White thinks the tenth drop will fall in the next few years. He would be happy with a good video of it.

vocab.en: an important stage or event in development
vocab.example: Reaching 10,000 subscribers was a major milestone for her podcast.

vocab.en: to start or establish something
vocab.example: They set up a small business selling handmade candles.

vocab.en: so slight or slow that it can hardly be noticed
vocab.example: There was an almost imperceptible change in his tone of voice.

vocab.en: a person responsible for looking after something
vocab.example: The museum sees itself as the custodian of the city's history.

vocab.en: thick and sticky, so it flows slowly
vocab.example: Honey becomes more viscous when it is stored in the fridge.

vocab.en: to pass without being noticed or caught
vocab.example: The deadline slipped past while we were busy with other projects.

vocab.en: a person who held a job or position before someone else
vocab.example: The new manager is far more relaxed than her predecessor.

vocab.en: to stop something from succeeding
vocab.example: Heavy rain foiled our plans for a picnic.

vocab.en: to accept something less than you hoped for
vocab.example: We wanted a house with a garden but had to settle for a flat.

questions.q: Thomas Parnell cut the bottom off the funnel three years after sealing the pitch inside it.
questions.explain: 原文称 In 1927 he heated a batch... Three years later he cut off the bottom of the funnel，与题干一致，故为True。

questions.q: John Mainstone finally saw a drop fall in 1979.
questions.explain: 原文称 only for a drop to fall after he had gone home，说明他错过了，与题干矛盾，故为False。

questions.q: The university plans to install cameras from several different angles to capture the tenth drop.
questions.explain: 原文只说 White would settle for a really good recording，并未提到多角度摄像机计划，故为Not Given。

questions.q: Why did the 2014 drop not fall cleanly?
options: The air conditioning was switched off
The beaker below was already crowded with earlier pitch
A power cut stopped the experiment
questions.explain: 原文称 the beaker beneath was already crowded with earlier pitch，故选C。

stories.discuss: Why do you think people are so fascinated by slow, long-term experiments like this one? Are projects without quick results still worth funding today?

stories.headline: Australian schools head for a digital detox with less screen time
stories.headlineZh: 澳大利亚学校将推行“数字排毒”，减少屏幕时间
stories.summaryZh: 各级教育部长同意成立专责小组，限制屏幕使用和小学生成式AI，引发对教学方式的讨论。
stories.c1:
After decades in which laptops and tablets steadily colonised Australian classrooms, the tide appears to be turning. Federal, state and territory education ministers have agreed to consider national limits on screen use in schools, prompted by a federal report warning that digital technology, including artificial intelligence, could undermine children's critical thinking, concentration and problem-solving.

Under the plan, generative AI will be restricted in primary schools and in high school assessments, and some Year 5 NAPLAN tests, which are currently all completed online, will return to pen and paper. A new taskforce on digital detoxing will report to ministers three times next year. The move builds on screen time limits already flagged in NSW and Victoria and follows similar steps in Norway and New York. Education Minister Jason Clare has insisted he is not out to scrap iPads, but sees a strong case for more pen and paper and less tech.

Writing in The Conversation, educational psychologist Jason Lodge describes the report as a step in the right direction, while cautioning that more planning is needed. The research, he notes, is far from clear-cut. The OECD has found that 15-year-olds who use devices moderately for learning outperform both heavy users and non-users, and countries that poured money into school computers saw no meaningful gains in reading, maths or science. Technology tends to help, he argues, when it is used for specific purposes, such as targeted practice or precise feedback.

Lodge also points out that there is no comprehensive national data on how long students spend on devices at school, and that rules vary widely from school to school. With AI almost unavoidable in daily life, the taskforce's real challenge will be deciding when, rather than whether, technology belongs in the classroom.
stories.b2:
For many years, laptops and tablets have become more and more common in Australian classrooms. Now that may change. Education ministers from the federal government and the states and territories have agreed to consider national limits on screen use in schools. A federal report warned that technology, including AI, could harm children's thinking, concentration and problem-solving.

Under the plan, generative AI will be limited in primary schools and in high school tests. Some Year 5 NAPLAN tests will go back to pen and paper. A new taskforce will report to ministers three times next year. NSW and Victoria have already talked about screen limits. Education Minister Jason Clare says he does not want to get rid of iPads, but he wants more pen and paper.

Education expert Jason Lodge says the report is a good start, but more planning is needed. He says the research is mixed. Students who use devices a moderate amount for learning do better than heavy users and non-users. Technology helps most when it has a clear purpose, such as practice or feedback.

Lodge also says there is no national data on how much time students spend on devices at school. Rules are also different in each school. He thinks the main question is when technology should be used in class.

vocab.en: a situation or trend is starting to change
vocab.example: After years of decline, the tide is turning for local bookshops.
forms: the tide appears to be turning

vocab.en: to gradually make something weaker or less effective

vocab.en: to use an earlier success as a base for further progress

vocab.en: to give reasons why something is a good idea

vocab.word: a step in the right direction
vocab.zh: 朝正确方向迈出的一步
vocab.en: an action that helps, though more is needed
vocab.example: The new bike lanes are a step in the right direction for the city.

vocab.en: simple and certain, with no doubt
vocab.example: The choice between the two jobs wasn't as clear-cut as I'd hoped.

vocab.en: to spend a lot of money on something
vocab.example: The council has poured money into the new sports centre.

vocab.en: to do better than others
vocab.example: Small investors sometimes outperform professional fund managers.

vocab.en: including all or nearly all details
vocab.example: The guide gives a comprehensive overview of renting in Melbourne.

questions.q: All Year 5 NAPLAN tests are currently completed online.
questions.explain: 原文称 some Year 5 NAPLAN tests, which are currently all completed online，说明目前全部在线完成，故为True。

questions.q: Jason Clare wants to remove iPads from all classrooms.
questions.explain: 原文称 he is not out to scrap iPads，与题干矛盾，故为False。

questions.q: Most parents surveyed support the new screen time limits.
questions.explain: 原文没有提及家长调查或家长支持率，故为Not Given。

questions.q: According to Jason Lodge, when is technology most likely to help learning?
options: When students use it for as long as possible
When it replaces teachers in primary schools
When it is used for specific purposes such as targeted practice
When schools stop using pen and paper
questions.explain: 原文称 Technology tends to help... when it is used for specific purposes, such as targeted practice or precise feedback，故选C。

stories.discuss: Do you think reducing technology in classrooms will help students learn better? How might schools balance traditional skills with preparing students for a digital world?

dialogue.title: Prepping for the Big Interview
dialogue.setting: Two housemates in Footscray run through practice questions the night before one of them has a job interview.
dialogue.settingZh: 两位住在Footscray的室友在面试前一晚一起练习面试问题。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Thanks for doing this, Declan. I'm honestly a bundle of nerves about tomorrow.
lines.zh: 谢谢你帮我，Declan。说实话，我对明天紧张得要命。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Happy to help. Right, let's kick off with the classic: tell me about yourself.
lines.zh: 乐意帮忙。好，咱们从经典问题开始：介绍一下你自己。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Okay, so I've got three years in marketing, mostly working on social media campaigns.
lines.zh: 好的，我有三年市场营销经验，主要做社交媒体推广活动。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Not bad, but you're underselling yourself. Mention the campaign that went viral last year.
lines.zh: 还不错，但你太低估自己了。提一下去年那个爆红的推广活动。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Fair point. I always feel like I'm blowing my own trumpet when I bring that up.
lines.zh: 有道理。每次提那个我都觉得自己在自吹自擂。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: That's literally the point of an interview. Own it — they want to hear the wins.
lines.zh: 面试本来就是干这个的。大方承认吧——他们就想听你的成绩。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Alright. What if they ask about my biggest weakness? I always draw a blank.
lines.zh: 好吧。要是他们问我最大的缺点呢？我每次都脑子一片空白。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Pick something real but fixable, then explain what you're doing to work on it.
lines.zh: 选一个真实但能改进的缺点，再说说你在怎么改。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Maybe that I tend to take on too much and struggle to say no?
lines.zh: 也许可以说我常常揽太多活，不太会拒绝？

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Perfect, as long as you follow it up with how you've learnt to prioritise.
lines.zh: 很好，只要你接着说说你是怎么学会分清轻重缓急的。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Got it. And should I ask them anything at the end, or just wrap things up?
lines.zh: 明白了。最后我应该问他们问题吗，还是直接结束？

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Definitely ask something. Ask what success looks like in the first six months.
lines.zh: 一定要问。问问他们入职头六个月怎样算做得好。

lines.name: Anika
lines.en: Ooh, that's a good one. I'm starting to feel a lot less rattled now.
lines.zh: 哦，这个问题好。我现在感觉没那么慌了。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: You'll smash it. Just get a decent night's sleep and don't overthink it.
lines.zh: 你肯定没问题。好好睡一觉，别想太多。

phrases.en: I'm honestly a bundle of nerves
phrases.zh: a bundle of nerves 形容非常紧张
kick off 开始，口语常用

phrases.plain: you don't describe yourself well enough
phrases.zh: undersell oneself 低估、少说自己的优点
blow one's own trumpet 自吹自擂
draw a blank 脑子一片空白
smash it 澳式口语：表现出色
